nameStory: The Band-rumped Storm-Petrel gets its name from the distinctive white band across its rump that's visible when the bird is in flight. It's also called the Madeiran Storm-Petrel after the island of Madeira where it was first scientifically described. The 'storm-petrel' part comes from sailors' observations of these tiny seabirds that seem to dance across stormy ocean waves.
description: The Band-rumped Storm-Petrel is a small, dark seabird about the size of a large swallow, with a wingspan around 17 inches. These ocean wanderers spend almost their entire lives at sea, only coming to land to nest on remote islands. They're sooty black above with a crisp white band across the rump, and have a distinctive bouncing flight pattern as they pick food from the ocean surface. In New England waters, they're extremely rare visitors, with only one confirmed sighting on record.

idTips.label: White rump band
idTips.description: Look for a clean, bright white band that wraps completely around the rump - it's much more defined and square-cut than the patchy white on similar species

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with shallow wingbeats and long glides, often appearing to bounce or skip across the water surface rather than fluttering constantly

idTips.label: Overall coloring
idTips.description: Deep sooty black or dark brown above with slightly paler underparts - looks uniformly dark except for the white rump when seen from a distance

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Compact and swallow-like with relatively broad, triangular wings and a notched tail that's often held closed in a point

idTips.label: Ocean behavior
idTips.description: Patters feet on water surface while picking up small fish and plankton - never dives completely under like other seabirds

habitat: In New England waters, Band-rumped Storm-Petrels would be found far offshore in deep ocean waters, typically many miles from the continental shelf. They prefer warm ocean currents and are most likely encountered during or after major storms that blow pelagic birds closer to shore. Any sighting would likely be from a whale-watching boat or during specialized pelagic birding trips in late summer or fall.

seasonality.spring: Extremely unlikely to be seen in New England waters during spring migration periods.
seasonality.summer: Best chance for sightings during late summer when tropical storms or hurricanes might carry birds northward into New England waters.
seasonality.fall: Possible vagrant during fall migration, especially after major storm systems move through the region in August or September.
seasonality.winter: Not expected in New England waters during winter months as they retreat to warmer tropical and subtropical oceans.

funFact: Band-rumped Storm-Petrels can live for over 30 years despite weighing less than a AA battery, and they have special salt glands that allow them to drink seawater and sneeze out the excess salt through their nostrils!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Leach's Storm-Petrel, which is much more common in New England waters. Remember that Band-rumped has a clean, complete white rump band like a white belt, while Leach's has a divided white rump patch that looks like white suspenders with a dark line down the middle.
contextualKnowledge: This species has multiple common names including Madeiran Storm-Petrel and Harcourt's Storm-Petrel, which can cause confusion in field guides and birding reports. The scientific name 'castro' honors Portuguese naturalist João de Castro, not the more famous political figure many people assume.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative Leach's Storm-Petrel (the only other species in the same genus found in New England), Band-rumped Storm-Petrel has a complete white rump band rather than a divided one, and flies with more gliding and less erratic fluttering. Band-rumped also has broader wings and appears more compact overall, with less of the bouncy, bat-like flight that characterizes Leach's Storm-Petrel.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Leach's Storm-Petrel differs from its close relative the Band-rumped Storm-Petrel by having a more deeply forked tail and more erratic, bat-like flight pattern, while Band-rumped flies more steadily with shallower wingbeats.
